title: THE BIBLE’S MOST SENSUAL BOOK: Why Is Song of Solomon in Scripture?
paragraphs:
THE BIBLE’S MOST SENSUAL BOOK: Why Is Song of Solomon in Scripture?
The book that talks about kisses, bodies, desire, longing, marriage, and love without apologizing—and the reason God refused to leave it out of His Word.
There is a book in your Bible that begins with a kiss.
Not a battle.
Not a miracle.
Not a commandment.
Not a sermon about judgment.
A kiss.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth…”
And suddenly, some Christians become uncomfortable.
Because this does not sound like the language we expect to hear in church.
It sounds intimate.
It sounds passionate.
It sounds almost too human.

And as the poetry continues, it becomes even more startling. A man admires the beauty of a woman. A woman longs for the man she loves. They speak of fragrance, lips, embraces, breasts, gardens, desire, separation, longing, belonging, and consummated love.
And God allowed all of it into Scripture.
That raises a question far more important than whether the Song of Solomon makes modern Christians uncomfortable.
Why is it there?
Why would the Holy Spirit preserve such intensely romantic poetry in the Bible?
And perhaps the question underneath that question is even more personal:
What if our discomfort with Song of Solomon reveals something we have misunderstood about God?
The Hebrew title is breathtaking in its simplicity:
שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים
Shir ha-Shirim.
Literally, “Song of Songs.”
It is a Hebrew superlative—the song above songs, the supreme song.
And then, almost immediately:
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu, ki-tovim dodekha miyyayin.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your love is better than wine.”
Song of Songs 1:2.
That is essentially what the Hebrew says. There is no need to sanitize it.
The Bible does not.
The poem is sensual because embodied human love is part of the world God created.

That does not mean every form of sexual desire is therefore holy. Scripture places sexual union within a larger biblical theology of covenant, faithfulness, holiness, self-giving love, and marriage. Jesus Himself reaches back to creation when speaking about marriage: “the two shall become one flesh” (Matthew 19:4–6; cf. Genesis 2:24).
But Christianity has never needed to pretend the body itself is evil.
The body is God's creation.
Marriage is God's creation.
Human sexuality is God's creation.
And sin did not create desire.
Sin distorted what God created.
That distinction changes everything.
Some people have been taught, explicitly or implicitly, that holiness means becoming embarrassed by embodiment.
Song of Songs refuses to cooperate.
The lovers notice each other.
They desire each other.
They miss each other.
They delight in one another.
The woman has a voice, longing, agency, and desire of her own. She is not merely an object being observed. Again and again she speaks.
“My beloved is mine, and I am his.”
Song of Songs 2:16.
Later comes one of the most famous declarations in the entire book:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְדוֹדִי לִי
Ani le-dodi ve-dodi li.
“I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine.”
Song of Songs 6:3.
Notice the mutuality.
Belonging meets belonging.
Love answers love.
This is not the language of exploitation.
It is the language of reciprocal delight.
And that matters enormously in a world that has repeatedly confused lust with love.
Lust asks:
“What can I take from you?”
Covenant love asks:
“How can I faithfully give myself to you?”
Pornography consumes bodies.
Biblical love recognizes persons.
Exploitation reduces someone to an appetite.
Covenant says, “You are my beloved.”
That may be one reason this ancient book feels strangely revolutionary in the modern world.
Our culture is simultaneously saturated with sexuality and starving for intimacy.
Bodies are everywhere.
Covenant is harder to find.
People can expose almost everything about themselves and still remain terrified of actually being known.
We swipe.
We scroll.
We compare.
We fantasize.
We consume.
We perform.
We hide.
And somewhere beneath all of it is an ancient human cry:
Does anybody see me and still want me?
Does anybody know me and remain?
Can I belong to someone without being consumed by them?
Can love survive when beauty changes?
Can desire become something more than appetite?
Song of Songs answers with poetry rather than a lecture.
And then, near its climax, the book says something astonishing:
“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm…”
Then comes the line generations have remembered:
כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה
Ki-azzah khamavet ahavah.
“For love is strong as death.”
Song of Songs 8:6.
Read that again.
Love is strong as death.
Not cheap.
Not disposable.
Not merely hormonal.
Not merely recreational.
Love lays claim upon the whole person.
And the poem continues with imagery of blazing fire before declaring that many waters cannot extinguish love and floods cannot sweep it away (Song of Songs 8:6–7).
Then comes an extraordinary statement about money:
If someone attempted to buy love with all the wealth of his house, he would be utterly despised.
Love cannot finally be purchased.
That sounds painfully relevant now.
You can purchase attention.
You can purchase an image.
You can purchase an experience.
You can purchase access.
You can purchase artificial intimacy.
But you cannot purchase covenant love.
Real love must be given.
And here the Song begins opening a door into something even larger.
Christians should be careful at this point.
Song of Songs is genuine love poetry. We do not honor Scripture by pretending its human lovers and embodied imagery are not really there.
But neither should Christians read any biblical book as though it existed in isolation from the rest of Scripture.

Throughout the Bible, marriage becomes one of the great images used to describe God's covenant relationship with His people. The prophets use marital imagery concerning the LORD and Israel. In the New Testament, Christ is presented as the Bridegroom, and the church as His bride. Paul explicitly uses marriage to speak about Christ and the church in Ephesians 5:25–32. Revelation culminates in the marriage supper of the Lamb and the appearance of the Bride.
So Christians do not need to claim that every breast, kiss, garden, fragrance, or embrace in Song of Songs is a secret code about Jesus.
That can flatten the poem rather than honor it.
Something more beautiful is happening.
The human love celebrated in the Song exists inside a Bible whose ultimate story is about the covenant-making God pursuing, redeeming, cleansing, and finally dwelling with His people.
Human covenant love can therefore become a signpost.
Not the Savior.
A signpost.
Marriage cannot save you.
Romance cannot save you.
Sex cannot save you.
Finding “the one” cannot save you.
Another human being cannot carry the weight of being your god.
Eventually every earthly romance encounters weakness, misunderstanding, aging, disappointment, sickness, limitation, and death.
Even the most faithful marriage ends, in this age, when death separates husband and wife.
And suddenly the words become haunting:
“Love is strong as death.”
But the Gospel announces something Song of Songs by itself does not yet reveal in fullness.
Jesus Christ went into death.
And came back.
That is where Christian hope moves beyond romantic sentiment.
At the cross, we do not merely encounter an emotion called love.
We encounter love acting.
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8.
There is the scandal.
He knew what we were.
And He came anyway.
He knew the secret history.
The private compromises.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The affair.
The fantasy.
The bitterness.
The marriage barely surviving behind smiling photographs.
The loneliness hidden beneath jokes.
The shame attached to what happened to you.
The shame attached to what you did.
The years you cannot recover.
The promises you broke.
The person you used.
The person who used you.
The nights when you begged to be loved and settled for being wanted.
Jesus knew.
And the cross still happened.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God dealing with sin at an unimaginable cost to Himself.
Christ does not redeem us because we finally become attractive enough for Him.
He loves sinners and gives Himself to rescue them.
This is why the Gospel is infinitely deeper than the modern command to “love yourself.”
Christianity does not ultimately say, “Look inside yourself until you discover that you were enough all along.”
It says something far more startling:
You were a sinner who could not rescue yourself, and yet you were loved by a Savior who willingly gave Himself for you.
You do not need to pretend the stain is imaginary.
Jesus washes sinners.
You do not need to rename darkness as light.
Jesus brings people out of darkness.
You do not need to rewrite your history to make yourself innocent.
Jesus can redeem a guilty history.
Repentance is not the enemy of love.
Repentance is what happens when grace finally makes hiding unnecessary.
Maybe that is where this article stopped being about an unusual Old Testament book and started becoming about you.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to want love so desperately that you accepted something counterfeit.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once promised God you would never cross.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe somebody violated your trust and left you carrying shame that never belonged on your shoulders.
Maybe your marriage is cold.
Maybe your bed is empty.
Maybe your spouse is beside you, but somehow you have never felt farther apart.
Maybe you are single and tired of Christians treating marriage like the reward God gives people who finally become spiritual enough.
Maybe you are married and discovered that another human being cannot heal the deepest fracture in your soul.
Maybe you have confused being desired with being loved.
Maybe you have used another person because, for a few minutes, being wanted made the loneliness quieter.
Then morning came.
The screen went dark.
The door closed.
The conversation ended.
The secret remained.
And you were still hungry.
Listen carefully.
Your deepest hunger cannot be healed by pretending you do not have a body.
But neither can it be healed by worshiping your body.
You were made for God.
That is why every created pleasure becomes cruel when we demand that it become our Savior.
The Song celebrates created love.
The Gospel reveals redeeming Love.
And when those truths are kept in their proper places, something beautiful happens.
You can enjoy God's gifts without turning them into gods.
You can celebrate marriage without worshiping marriage.
You can acknowledge sexual desire without becoming its slave.
You can honor singleness without treating it as spiritual failure.
You can repent of sexual sin without believing sexual sin places you beyond Christ's mercy.
You can carry wounds without making those wounds your identity.
You can be honest.
Because Jesus already knows.
That may be the sentence somebody reading this needed tonight.
Jesus already knows.
And He is still calling sinners to come.
Not to remain unchanged.
To come and be changed.
The Jesus who said, “Come to Me,” is also the Jesus who says, “Follow Me.”
Grace does not merely comfort us inside our chains.
Grace begins breaking them.
Christ forgives.
Christ cleanses.
Christ restores.
Christ teaches us to love differently.
And perhaps this is where Song of Songs becomes unexpectedly confrontational.
Because the book asks whether we still believe love should be precious.
Whether another person's body should be treated as sacred rather than consumable.
Whether faithfulness still matters.
Whether waiting can sometimes be wisdom.
Three times the Song contains a recurring warning not to awaken or arouse love before its proper time (Song of Songs 2:7; 3:5; 8:4).
There is wisdom there.
Desire is powerful.
Fire is beautiful in a fireplace.
The same fire unleashed can burn a house to the ground.
The Christian response to desire is therefore neither worship nor disgust.
It is discipleship.
Bring your desires under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Bring your relationships there.
Bring your sexuality there.
Bring your marriage there.
Bring your singleness there.
Bring your memories there.
Bring your temptations there.
Bring your wounds there.
Bring the parts you keep editing out of your testimony.
Especially those.
Because Jesus has always been remarkably willing to enter stories respectable people would rather avoid.
A Samaritan woman with a complicated relational history.
A woman caught in adultery.
A prostitute weeping at His feet.
Tax collectors.
Outcasts.
The publicly disgraced.
The privately guilty.
And then the cross itself—the most scandalous place imaginable.
Public humiliation.
Nakedness.
Mockery.
Blood.
Condemnation.
Death.
And God turned the place of apparent defeat into the place from which forgiveness would be proclaimed to the nations.
That is the pattern of the Gospel.
Scandal does not get the final word.
Sin does not get the final word.
Shame does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming what sin tried to destroy.
So why is the Bible's most sensual book in Scripture?
Because God is not embarrassed by what He created.
Because covenant love matters.
Because bodies matter.
Because fidelity matters.
Because desire needs wisdom.
Because intimacy is more than consumption.
Because human love is beautiful but incapable of being God.
Because Scripture is honest enough to speak to the whole human person rather than merely the polished religious version we present on Sunday.

And because, when read within the whole sweep of Scripture, even the beauty of faithful human love can make the Christian heart ache for something greater—the final communion between Christ and His redeemed people.
The Bible begins with a marriage in a garden.
And near the end of Revelation, Scripture gives us another wedding.
“The marriage of the Lamb has come, and His wife has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7).
Then Scripture ends with God dwelling with His people.
No more death.
No more mourning.
No more crying.
No more pain.
The separation ends.
The longing ends.
The exile ends.
The Bridegroom has His Bride.
And suddenly an ancient book filled with longing does not seem so strange inside the Bible after all.
We are creatures who long.
We long to know.
To be known.
To belong.
To be loved without being consumed.
To be seen without being abandoned.
Every human romance whispers about that hunger, but none can completely satisfy it.
Only Christ can finally bring the sinner home to God.
So perhaps the question is no longer, “Why would God put Song of Solomon in the Bible?”
Perhaps the question is:
What have you been asking to satisfy a hunger that was always leading you toward Him?
If something hidden was exposed while you read this, do not run from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Do not let this article disappear into another endless scroll.
Come back when desire becomes confusing, when shame begins speaking again, or when somebody tells you Christianity is embarrassed by human sexuality.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ. But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one voluntary expression of stewardship when you genuinely believe that work is bearing good fruit.
It is to Christ.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you are hiding, come into the light.
If you have fallen, call upon Jesus.
If you have been wounded, bring the wound to Him.
If your desires have become your master, surrender them to the One who purchased you with His blood.
If you thought your scandal disqualified you from grace, look again at the cross.
Because the Gospel was never the story of impressive people making themselves worthy enough for God.
It is the story of a holy God rescuing sinners through the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
And maybe that is why one of Scripture's strangest, most sensual, most beautiful books belongs exactly where God placed it.
It reminds us that we were created to love.
The rest of Scripture teaches us how deeply that love has been wounded by sin.
And Jesus shows us what redeeming love ultimately costs.
A cross.
An empty tomb.
A Savior who still receives sinners.
So when shame whispers, “After everything you've done, who could possibly want you?”
Do not answer with your feelings.
Answer with Calvary.
The deepest love story in Scripture is not that you finally found someone worth loving—it is that, in Jesus Christ, holy Love came looking for sinners who could never save themselves.
